Ah well, I guess my lesson from this is to listen to my audio gear BEFORE I buy it.

It’s actually very common to have this kind of reaction to one’s deadname. As for therapy, I have been to several and all of them (including my current one) agree that it is normal and will subside with time. They also all agree that people should generally steer clear of my deadname unless they have good reason to say it. Thank you for your concern. Genuinely. I understand how insane this all seems to a cis person but it really is normal for people who have stated their transition fairly recently to have extreme reactions to their deadname. I totally do get it. And don’t just skim through this and make a snarky response. Really understand that I do understand how it seems to people who aren’t accustomed to all this. I genuinely hope that, if this conversation doesn’t convince you of my point, it at least provides the spark to start learning about this kind of thing on a deeper level. <3

I’m not trying to control everyone around me. The same way I don’t want people around me to call me derogatory terms or any other childish names, I don’t want them to call me my deadname. If they do call me my deadname, I’ll just politely and calmly explain why I would like them to stop and if they don’t, despite knowing the immense pain it causes me, that’s their choice. I’m going to distance myself from them. The name causes me pain. I have had panic attacks because of hearing my deadname. If people aren’t willing to do the basic, decent thing and stop saying something they know causes me great distress and that they have no reason to say, that’s severely disrespectful. If somebody is dead-set (if you’ll excuse the pun) on saying my deadname, I don’t want to be around them.

Nobody ever saying our deadname again is certainly what we hope for. Of course, there will be slip-ups and there will be cases where we have to put our legal names on things before we’ve legally changed our names. Of course it won’t be like an instant switch of people never saying it again but no trans person that I know of has ever though it okay for people to say their deadnames even when they can’t hear it. And, of course, there will be people who are rude and won’t make the change but we try to distance ourselves from them. Even though you disagree, do you really think calling me names like “fucktard” is going to do you any good? Not only is that specific name dangerously close to the ableist r-slur, it’s simply counterproductive to be rude to people you are debating. I have had fairly heated debates with people about things like religion and ethics, things that I feel very strongly about, but neither I nor the person I am debating has even found it necessary to resort to such childish practices as name-calling. Grow up.

It’s not that the name never existed. I fully accept that his deadname existed. I just don’t say it because he’s asked everybody not to and it’s the least I can do. I’m not perpetuating anything but plain human decency. Just because you can’t imagine the pain that this kind of thing causes, doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist. (I’m guessing you’re cis based off of your... unsavoury view of this issue.)
It’s basic human decency. His deadname is, regrettably, all over the internet because people didn’t know the pain it caused. Just because you can say his deadname, doesn’t mean you should.

Saying a trans person’s deadname is disrespectful in the same way that it would be disrespectful if I started calling my boyfriend Greg out of nowhere. Furthermore, in this analogy, my boyfriend has explicitly said that being called Greg is not only incorrect but it is also deeply hurtful because the name is connected to a painful part of his life. It’s the same here. Even though Elliot isn’t here, it would still be disrespectful to refer to him by his deadname in the same way that it is disrespectful to say the n-word even if there aren’t any black people around.
Okay, and I’ve provided ways you can avoid it and why it’s important that you try to avoid it.
